1.s: Paul greets the Roman church and says he is not ashamed of the good news, “the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes.” Humanity has exchanged the truth of God for idols.
1.d: Like other New Testament letters, Romans opens by naming the writer and readers and giving thanks; 1:16–17 then states the theme [[tosn:Romans 1:1-17]]: the good news is God’s power to save everyone who believes, for “the righteous shall live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4) [[bible:Romans 1:16-17]].

2.s: God judges everyone impartially, Jews and Gentiles alike. True circumcision is of the heart.
2.d: Those who judge others do the same things: Jews as well as Gentiles turn from what God has shown them [[tosn:Romans 2:1-5]]. Only God judges fairly, and he sees even people’s thoughts [[bsn:Romans 2:1-16]] [[tosn:Romans 2:16]].

3.s: “All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” But now God’s righteousness is revealed through faith in Jesus Christ, and people are justified freely by his grace.
3.d: Paul strings psalms together to show that all people are under the power of sin [[tosn:Romans 3:10-12]] [[tosn:Romans 3:10-18]]: “all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” [[bible:Romans 3:23]]. In 3:21–26 he states most clearly that God’s righteousness is revealed in Jesus Christ for everyone who believes [[tosn:Romans 3:21-4:25]]. “Atoning sacrifice” recalls the mercy seat on the ark, the centre of the Day of Atonement [[tosn:Romans 3:25]].

4.s: Abraham was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe.
4.d: Abraham trusted God’s promise, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6), before he was circumcised [[tosn:Romans 4:3]] [[tosn:Romans 4:10]]. He did nothing to earn the promise [[bsn:Romans 4:1-25]]; he believed God, “who gives life to the dead” [[bible:Romans 4:17]].

5.s: Being justified by faith, we have peace with God. “God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Adam brought death; Christ brings life.
5.d: Adam’s name also means “human”, and Paul contrasts the one man whose sin brought death to all with the one man, Christ, whose obedience brings life [[tosn:Romans 5:12]] [[tosn:Romans 5:15]]. Believers have been moved from the realm of Adam to the realm of Christ [[tosn:Romans 5:1-8:39]].

6.s: Shall we keep sinning so grace may increase? No: in baptism we died with Christ and rose to new life. “The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life.”
6.d: If grace abounds where sin abounds, does sin not matter? Paul answers no [[tosn:Romans 6:1]]: the power to live a new life comes from being united with Christ in his death, burial and resurrection [[tosn:Romans 6:4]], pictured in baptism [[tosn:Romans 6:3]].

7.s: Believers are freed from the law. Paul describes the struggle: “The good which I desire, I don’t do.” “Who will deliver me?… I thank God through Jesus Christ.”
7.d: The law itself is good, but sin uses it [[tosn:Romans 7:7-25]]. Christians have long differed over whether “I” in 7:14–25 describes Paul’s life before God rescued him, or the part of a believer that still resists God’s will [[tosn:Romans 7:18]].

8.s: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” The Spirit makes us children of God who cry “Abba, Father”. Creation groans for redemption. “All things work together for good.” Nothing can separate us from God’s love.
8.d: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” [[bible:Romans 8:1]]: neither sin nor the law can keep believers from eternal life [[tosn:Romans 8:1]]. The Spirit, named nineteen times in this chapter [[bible:Romans 8:1-27]], guides Christians and helps them resist sin [[tosn:Romans 8:9]]. Nothing can separate us from God’s love in Christ [[bible:Romans 8:38-39]].

9.s: Paul grieves for his fellow Jews. God’s promise has not failed: not all descended from Israel are Israel. God has mercy on whom he will have mercy.
9.d: Paul grieves for Israel, God’s covenant people [[tosn:Romans 9:4]]. The difference between Jacob and Esau came from God’s choice, not from anything they did [[tosn:Romans 9:10-11]]; Christians have long wrestled with this hard teaching about God’s choosing.

10.s: “If you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace”
10.d: “If you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord… you will be saved” [[bible:Romans 10:9]]. Paul applies Deuteronomy 30:12–14 to the good news [[tosn:Romans 10:6-8]], and Joel’s “the LORD” to Jesus [[tosn:Romans 10:13]].

11.s: God has not rejected Israel. Gentiles are grafted into the olive tree; one day “all Israel will be saved”. “Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God!”
11.d: Not all Israel has rejected the Messiah [[bsn:Romans 11:1-24]]. The olive tree, already a picture of Israel in the Old Testament, warns Gentile believers against pride: they share in blessings rooted in God’s promises to Israel [[tosn:Romans 11:17-24]] [[tosn:Romans 11:18]]. “All Israel” can be understood more than one way [[tosn:Romans 11:26-27]].

12.s: “Present your bodies a living sacrifice.” Be transformed by renewing your mind. Use your gifts. Love sincerely; bless those who persecute you; overcome evil with good.
12.d: “Therefore… present your bodies a living sacrifice” [[bible:Romans 12:1]]: the letter turns from teaching to living. Much in Romans 12–13 closely reflects the teaching of Jesus [[tosn:Romans 12:14]].

13.s: Submit to governing authorities. “Owe no one anything, except to love one another.” Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
13.d: Christians submit to governing authorities, whom God appoints to keep order and justice, but always under their first obedience to God [[tosn:Romans 13:1-2]] [[bsn:Romans 13:1-7]]. “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” [[bible:Romans 13:8]].

14.s: Don’t judge one another over food or special days. Each will give account to God; don’t make others stumble.
14.d: “Weak” faith means a sensitive conscience about things Christian freedom allows [[tosn:Romans 14:1]]. The strong must not pressure others to act against their conscience [[tosn:Romans 14:14]], and believers must not quarrel over such differences [[bsn:Romans 14:1-23]].

15.s: The strong should bear with the weak, as Christ did. Paul’s mission plans: to Jerusalem with a gift, then to Rome and Spain.
15.d: Through Christ, Jews and Gentiles are united to glorify God as one people [[tosn:Romans 15:8-9]]; Paul strings Old Testament texts together to show Gentiles praising God [[tosn:Romans 15:9-12]].

16.s: Greetings to many friends, including Phoebe, a deacon, Prisca and Aquila, and Junia, “notable among the apostles”.
16.d: Paul greets twenty-seven Christians in Rome, ten of them women, which shows the important roles women played [[tosn:Romans 16:1-16]]. The names show a diverse church: Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free [[tosn:Romans 16:3-16]]. The name Junia can be read as a woman’s name [[tosn:Romans 16:7]].
